Blackbody Radiation

Planck’s law · Wien’s law · σT⁴

Clip Capture
Planck’s law · Wien’s law · Stefan–Boltzmann

Heat anything enough and it glows
red, then white, then blue, but never green.

Everything radiates because it is warm; you glow too, in the infrared, which is how a thermal camera sees you in the dark. Heat a body and its glow climbs into the visible, from dull red through orange and white to blue-white, while its power grows as the fourth power of the temperature. Classical physics predicted that every hot coal should blaze with unlimited ultraviolet. Planck fixed it in 1900 by letting energy come in lumps, $E = hf$, and quantum physics began.

Live: a body heated from 700 K to 7,000 K and back. Its glow goes from dull red through orange and white to blue-white, never green, while the peak of its spectrum slides to shorter wavelengths and the curve grows as $T^4$.

The glowA hotter body glows brighter and bluer; its spectrum peaks at Wien’s $λ_{max} = b/T$, $b = 2.898$ mm·K, and nothing glows green.
Power as T⁴Each square meter radiates $εσT^4$, and a body in surroundings at $T_s$ loses $εσA(T^4 - T_s^4)$ net.
Planck’s quantaThe classical law runs away in the ultraviolet; energy in steps of $E = hf$ cuts it off and gives Planck’s law.
Reading the skyA star’s color gives its temperature, its luminosity and temperature give its radius, and the CMB is a near-perfect blackbody at 2.725 K.

GuideBlackbody Radiation

About 10 minutes for Part 1 and 10 for Part 2.

Contents

This Guide covers the ideas and equations behind every Walkthrough step, Concept Challenge question and Predict round. Read Part 1 before the Intro track and Part 2 before the Advanced track, about ten minutes each. Come back whenever a question sends you here.

Part 1 · The essentials

Math you’ll need: algebra, powers and scientific notation; no calculus.

The big idea

Everything radiates because it is warm. The atoms of any body jostle with thermal energy, and moving charges emit light. A blackbody absorbs all the light that falls on it; a small hole in a closed, heated cavity is one, since light that enters is lost inside. Its glow depends on its temperature alone: its color, where its spectrum peaks and how much power it sends out all follow T, in kelvins. Real surfaces emit a fraction of a blackbody’s glow.

The glow and its color

Heat a body slowly and it first glows a dull red, near 800 K, then orange and white, and a very hot star is blue-white. (A lamp’s filament stops near 3,000 K, a pale orange that looks white only to an eye used to lamplight.) The spectrum is a broad hump of light at every wavelength. At low temperatures only its short-wavelength tail reaches the visible, at the red end; as T rises the whole curve grows and its peak slides toward shorter wavelengths, so more of the visible is filled and the mix whitens.

A blackbody’s thermal glow never looks green. (An LED, a fluorescent dye or a gas’s spectral line can be green: their light comes in a narrow band, not a blackbody’s broad hump.) At about 5,800 K the peak sits in the blue-green, near 500 nm, but the curve is so broad that red, green and blue arrive in nearly equal amounts, and that mix is white. Every blackbody’s color lies on one path, the Planckian locus, from red through orange and white to blue-white, and it never passes through green.

Where the spectrum peaks: Wien’s law

The wavelength where a blackbody’s spectrum is strongest is inversely proportional to its temperature, Wien’s displacement law:

$λ_{max}T = b$  $b = 2.898 × 10^{−3}$ m·K

T must be in kelvins: $T = T_C + 273.15$. Run backward, the law turns a measured peak into a temperature; that is how astronomers read a star’s.

Worked example. A kiln at 1,500 K peaks at $2.898 × 10^{−3}$ / 1,500 = 1.93 µm, in the infrared: its orange glow is only the curve’s tail. A body whose spectrum peaks at 600 nm is at $2.898 × 10^{−3}$ / ($6.00 × 10^{−7}$) = 4,830 K.

The power: Stefan’s law and net exchange

Each square meter of a blackbody radiates $σT^4$ in all, the area under its curve. A real surface radiates the fraction ε, its emissivity (0 to 1: matte black near 1, polished metal near 0.1):

$P = εσAT^4$  $σ = 5.670 × 10^{−8}$ W m⁻² K⁻⁴

The fourth power makes temperature matter enormously: twice the temperature, sixteen times the power. A body also absorbs what its surroundings radiate to it, so a small body at T in surroundings at $T_s$ loses, net,

$P_{net} = εσA(T^4 − T_s^4)$

At the surroundings’ temperature it still radiates, but absorbs just as much: the net is zero.

Worked example. Heat a body by a quarter, from 1,000 K to 1,250 K, and its power rises $1.25^4$ = 2.44 times. A large radiator panel, ε = 0.90, 3.0 m², at 345 K emits 0.90 × $5.670 × 10^{−8}$ × 3.0 × $345^4$ = 2,170 W; with the walls at 293 K it absorbs 1,130 W of theirs and loses 1,040 W net.

Everyday infrared

You glow too. Your skin, at about 307 K (34 °C), peaks at $b/T$ ≈ 9.4 µm, far in the infrared, which a thermal camera images in the 8–14 µm band. It reads each surface’s temperature from what arrives, assuming an emissivity; a shiny object fools it, since it emits little and mostly reflects the room. A mug of coffee at 333 K peaks at 8.7 µm; under ordinary viewing, nothing below about 800 K glows visibly. Planck’s curve has a visible tail at every temperature, but below that it is far too faint for the eye, even in the dark.

A light bulb is mostly a heater. Its filament’s peak lies in the infrared, and only the short-wavelength tail of the curve is visible.

Worked example. A halogen lamp at 3,200 K peaks at 906 nm, just beyond the red, and 10.5 % of its power falls between 400 and 700 nm; the rest is infrared.

The ultraviolet catastrophe and Planck’s quanta

Classical physics treated the light in a hot cavity as standing waves, each with the same average energy, kT. Short wavelengths fit in far more ways than long ones, so the predicted spectrum, the Rayleigh–Jeans law, rises without limit as λ shrinks:

$I(λ, T) = 2πckT/λ^4$

Its total power is infinite: the ultraviolet catastrophe, as Paul Ehrenfest named it in 1911 (Rayleigh worked out the law in 1900, Jeans corrected its factor in 1905). It matches the measurements only at long wavelengths.

In 1900 Max Planck, fitting careful infrared measurements, assumed that an oscillator in the cavity’s walls, of frequency f, can hold energy only in steps of hf, with $h = 6.626 × 10^{−34}$ J·s. (Einstein went further in 1905 and treated light itself as quanta, photons, each carrying hf.)

$E = hf = hc/λ$

When a step is much larger than kT, the oscillator almost never gets even one: the chance is about $e^{−hf/kT}$. Short wavelengths are frozen out, the curve turns down, and the result, Planck’s law, fits every measurement:

$I(λ, T) = \frac{2πhc^2}{λ^5}\frac{1}{e^{hc/λkT} − 1}$

Worked example. Light of 780 nm carries $hc/λ$ = $2.55 × 10^{−19}$ J = 1.59 eV per quantum. At 3,000 K, kT = 0.259 eV, so at 350 nm a quantum (3.54 eV) is 13.7 kT, and the chance of one is about $e^{−13.7}$, one in a million.

Part 2 · Going further

Math you’ll need: exponentials, and integrals read as areas, with their results given.

Planck’s law from modes

A cubic cavity of side L with conducting walls holds standing waves with wave numbers $(π/L)(n_x, n_y, n_z)$, two polarizations each. Those below a frequency ν fill an octant of a sphere of radius $2Lν/c$ in n-space, so they number $(8π/3)Vν^3/c^3$, and per unit frequency $8πVν^2/c^3$: more and more at high frequency. An exact count differs slightly: for light the walls’ terms cancel, leaving a term from the cube’s edges (about $3Lν/c$) and the lattice’s scatter, so the count approaches the formula as ν grows, sometimes from above.

$N(ν) = (8π/3)Vν^3/c^3$

A mode whose energy comes in steps of hν, with Boltzmann weights $e^{−nhν/kT}$, holds on average

$\bar{E} = hν/(e^{hν/kT} − 1)$

which is kT for $hν ≪ kT$ (equipartition) and $hν\,e^{−hν/kT}$, nearly zero, for $hν ≫ kT$. Modes per volume per frequency times mean energy gives Planck’s law as an energy density, $u_ν = (8πν^2/c^3)\bar{E}$, and $I_ν = (c/4)u_ν$.

Worked example. A 3 µm cube has about 765 modes below 450 THz by the formula; the exact count is 754. At 150 THz and 2,500 K, $hν/kT$ = 2.88 and $\bar{E}$ = 0.171 kT.

Two limits, and two peaks

With $x = hc/λkT$: for $x ≪ 1$, $e^x − 1 ≈ x$ and Planck’s law becomes Rayleigh–Jeans; for $x ≫ 1$ the −1 is negligible and it becomes Wien’s approximation, $(2πhc^2/λ^5)e^{−x}$. At the peak, x = 4.965, Wien’s is only 0.7 % low while Rayleigh–Jeans is 29 times too high.

Per unit frequency the spectrum peaks at x = 2.821:

$ν_{peak} = 2.821\,kT/h$

so $c/ν_{peak}$ is 1.76 times $λ_{max}$. A band of frequency and a band of wavelength are different slices, $dν = c\,dλ/λ^2$; neither peak is “the” peak.

Worked example. A 7,000 K star peaks at 414 nm per wavelength, but per frequency at $5.879 × 10^{10}$ × 7,000 Hz, whose wavelength is 728 nm.

σ and the photons, from the integrals

Integrated over all wavelengths with $x = hc/λkT$, Planck’s law gives $(2πk^4T^4/c^2h^3)∫_0^∞ x^3/(e^x − 1)\,dx$, and the integral is $π^4/15$:

$σ = 2π^5k^4/(15c^2h^3)$

The $T^4$ is about $T^3$ modes with $hν ≲ kT$, each holding about kT. A quarter of the power, always, lies at wavelengths shorter than $λ_{max}$. Counting photons instead, the flux is $4πζ(3)(kT)^3/(h^3c^2)$ per square meter, so the mean photon energy is

$π^4kT/(30ζ(3)) = 2.701\,kT$

a little below 2.821 kT, the photon energy at the peak of the per-frequency spectrum. “The most common photon” depends on how the spectrum is sliced: counted per unit energy, photons are most numerous near 1.59 kT.

Worked example. A 1,500 K body’s photons carry 2.701 × $8.617 × 10^{−5}$ × 1,500 = 0.349 eV on average. The Sun’s surface sends out $2.92 × 10^{26}$ photons per second from each square meter.

Emissivity and Kirchhoff’s law

Kirchhoff’s law: at each wavelength, a surface’s emissivity equals its absorptivity. A good absorber is a good emitter; a mirror emits little. Inside a cavity at one temperature, every opaque body’s emission plus its reflection of the walls is exactly the blackbody glow, so objects in a furnace vanish against its walls. A gray body has one ε at every wavelength: the blackbody’s shape and peak, scaled down,

$ε = P/(σAT^4)$

A selective emitter is different. Tungsten’s emissivity falls with wavelength, which tilts its spectrum toward the blue: a blackbody fitted to it reads a color temperature above the true one.

Worked example. A 2 cm² sample at 900 K radiating 1.2 W has ε = 1.2 / ($5.670 × 10^{−8}$ × $2 × 10^{−4}$ × $900^4$) = 0.161. Tungsten at 2,500 K radiates 0.277 of a blackbody’s total, and its spectrum fits as a 2,598 K blackbody.

Stars: temperature from color, radius from luminosity

Treated as a blackbody at its effective temperature, a star’s color gives T: by its peak, or by its color index B − V, which compares its brightness through blue and visual filters (larger is cooler). Its luminosity, from its brightness and distance, then gives its radius, since $L = 4πR^2σT^4$:

$R/R_⊙ = \sqrt{L/L_⊙}\,(T_⊙/T)^2$

with $T_⊙$ = 5,772 K. Cool and luminous means huge (a red giant); hot and faint means tiny (a white dwarf, the size of Earth). Real stars’ spectra have absorption lines and are not quite a blackbody’s, so their measured colors differ from the model’s, in both directions.

Worked example. A giant at 3,500 K with 300 times the Sun’s luminosity has $R = \sqrt{300}$ × (5,772 / 3,500)² = 47 solar radii.

The cosmic microwave background

The CMB is the glow left from when the universe was hot and opaque: a blackbody at 2.725 K, brightest at wavelengths of a millimeter or two, in the microwaves, with about 411 photons in every cubic centimeter. COBE’s FIRAS instrument found it a blackbody to about 50 parts per million of its peak. As the universe expands every wavelength stretches with it; $λ_{max}T = b$ then keeps it a blackbody, cooler in proportion. Looking back to redshift z, when the universe was $1 + z$ times smaller,

$T(z) = 2.725(1 + z)$ K

Worked example. At z = 19 the CMB was 2.725 × 20 = 54.5 K, peaking at 3.2 THz. At z ≈ 1,100 it was a few thousand kelvin, the moment hydrogen formed and the universe became transparent.

Reference

Common mistakes

Part 1

  1. Temperatures in °C. Wien’s and Stefan’s laws need kelvins: add 273.15.
  2. “The peak is the color.” A body peaking at 700 nm glows orange-white, not red; a 5,800 K body peaking in the blue-green looks white.
  3. Power ∝ T. It is $T^4$: twice as hot, sixteen times the power.
  4. Forgetting what comes back. The net loss is $εσA(T^4 − T_s^4)$, not $εσAT^4$; and never $(T − T_s)^4$.
  5. Areas in cm². Convert to m² first.
  6. “Only hot things radiate.” Everything does; a cool body absorbs about as much as it emits.
  7. “There are fewer short-wavelength modes.” There are more; Planck’s cutoff comes from hf ≫ kT.
  8. Joules for electron volts. 1 eV = $1.602 × 10^{−19}$ J.

Part 2

  1. Taking $c/λ_{max}$ for $ν_{peak}$. They differ by 1.76.
  2. A blackbody fit as the true temperature of a selective emitter: it is the color temperature.

    The spectrum

    Field Manual

    What you are looking at

    The stage shows a body on the left, drawn in the color its own spectrum gives, in a dark window, and its spectrum on the right: $I(λ, T)$, the power each square meter emits per unit wavelength (OpenStax’s “intensity”), against wavelength, with the visible band under the axis and the peak, $λ_{max}$, marked. Color only shows each glow at full brightness once it is visible; Brightness tone-maps the surface’s luminance against an eye adapted to a lit room, so a 700 K body is black and a 1,000 K one a dim red. The dashed Classical curve is the Rayleigh–Jeans prediction. The Sandbox adds the spectrum per frequency or in photons, gray and selective emitters, a shaded band with its share, pinned curves, a thermal camera’s view of a room and the CIE 1931 color diagram with the Planckian locus.

    The Spectrometer Bench records a source’s spectrum with a spectrometer of limited range and resolution, counting photons with shot noise and a dark rate, and fits Planck’s law for the temperature. The Star Lab places stars on an HR diagram with lines of constant radius, shows each one’s glow, spectrum and B − V, and follows the cosmic microwave background back in time. The Mode Counter counts a cavity’s standing waves one by one and compares the classical kT per mode with Planck’s mean energy: the ultraviolet catastrophe made visible.

    The physics

    A blackbody absorbs everything that falls on it; a cavity with a small hole is one. Its spectrum depends on its temperature alone: Planck’s law, $I(λ, T) = 2πhc^2/λ^5 · 1/(e^{hc/λkT} − 1)$. Its peak follows Wien’s displacement law, $λ_{max}T = b = 2.898 × 10^{−3}$ m·K, and its total is Stefan’s law, $σT^4$ per square meter, with $σ = 2π^5k^4/(15c^2h^3) = 5.670 × 10^{−8}$ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. A real surface emits the fraction ε, its emissivity, which by Kirchhoff’s law equals the fraction it absorbs at each wavelength; a gray body has one ε at all wavelengths. A small body at T in surroundings at $T_s$ loses $εσA(T^4 − T_s^4)$ net.

    Classical physics gave each standing wave in a cavity the energy kT. There are $8πν^2/c^3$ of them per unit volume and frequency, so the energy density $(8πν^2/c^3)kT$ grows without limit with frequency: the Rayleigh–Jeans law and its ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck let an oscillator of frequency ν hold energy only in steps of hν. Its mean energy is then $hν/(e^{hν/kT} − 1)$, about kT when $hν ≪ kT$ and almost nothing when $hν ≫ kT$, and the product is Planck’s law. Counted per unit frequency the spectrum peaks at $ν_{peak} = 2.821\,kT/h$, not at $c/λ_{max}$; the photons number $4πζ(3)(kT)^3/(h^3c^2)$ per second per square meter, with a mean energy of 2.701 kT. A star’s luminosity is $L = 4πR^2σT^4$, so its temperature and luminosity give its radius, and the universe’s expansion keeps the CMB a blackbody, cooler in proportion: $T = 2.725(1 + z)$ K.

    The model

    Planck’s law, exactly. The constants h, c, k and e are the exact SI values (2019); σ is computed from them (5.670 374 419 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, checked against CODATA to 10⁻⁹) and b is CODATA’s 2.897 771 955 × 10⁻³ m·K, checked against the root of $x = 5(1 − e^{−x})$. The share of the power in any band comes from an exact series; spectra that are not blackbodies, and filters, are integrated by Gauss–Legendre quadrature from 0.03 to 50,000 times $b/T$, which reproduces $σT^4$ to better than one part in $10^{13}$.

    Color. The spectrum is summed against the CIE 1931 2° standard observer’s color-matching functions at 5 nm, 380–780 nm (CIE 015:2018), to X, Y and Z, then converted to sRGB (IEC 61966-2-1). The engine puts CIE Illuminant A (a 2,856 K blackbody) at x = 0.4476, y = 0.4075, as the CIE does, and the Planckian locus within 0.0002 of published values from 1,000 to 10,000 K. A chromaticity outside the sRGB gamut (a blackbody below about 1,900 K lies beyond sRGB’s red–green edge, a deeper orange-red than any screen shows) loses its impossible negative primaries, which moves it to the nearest color the screen can make, toward the red primary; the body view says so (“deeper than a screen shows”). Luminance is $683\,∫B_λ\bar{y}\,dλ$ cd/m².

    Emissivity. Gray bodies take any ε from 0.01 to 1. Two selective emitters are illustrative: tungsten, with ε falling from about 0.42 in the blue to 0.27 at 2 µm and 0.21 at 5 µm (smooth, not handbook data; its total at 2,800 K is about 0.29), and a selective solar absorber, black (ε near 0.95) below about 1.5 µm and shiny (ε near 0.05) beyond about 4 µm, crossing over near 2.5 µm. A blackbody fitted to the tungsten curve at 2,500 K on the silicon spectrometer reads about 2,598 K: its color temperature. Real tungsten’s excess is about half the model’s, and a fitted color temperature depends on the spectrometer’s range.

    The thermal camera integrates each object’s 8–14 µm emission, $εS(T)$, plus the room it reflects, $(1 − ε)S(T_{room})$, and reports the temperature that would give that signal at ε = 0.95, as a camera set to a typical emissivity does. The room’s temperatures and emissivities are illustrative everyday values (skin 34 °C at 0.97, a polished kettle at 95 °C and 0.08).

    The spectrometers (illustrative, typical of small fiber spectrometers): silicon, 350–1,050 nm in 5 nm pixels at 6 nm resolution, 20 counts a second of dark rate; InGaAs, 900–1,700 nm in 10 nm pixels at 12 nm, 400 a second; a student visible spectrometer, 400–700 nm. Each pixel’s mean count is the source’s photon spectrum through a Gaussian slit, times the response and the exposure, plus the dark rate; the counts are exact Poisson draws from seeded streams, and a pixel at the full well (65,000) is flagged and left out of the fit. The live preview and the recordings use separate streams, and each recording depends only on its data set and its number, so Record again repeats it and New data does not. The fit is the same model, with the temperature, a scale and the dark rate free, by maximum likelihood for Poisson counts (Fisher scoring), the dark frame included; its ± is from the Fisher information. A Monte Carlo of 600 records of a 1,500 K calibrator at 2 ms (peak counts near 60) found the fitted T unbiased, its scatter 1.01 times the mean reported ±, and 69.7 % of the ±1σ intervals covering the truth. When the source’s counts are lost in the dark rate’s noise (a signal-to-noise below 5, as for the calibrator below about 850 K at 20 ms) the bench says so, and a dark rate fitted at its bound of 0 is marked, with no standard error. The tungsten lamp runs at about 2,950 K at 12 V, $T = 300 + 2650(V/12)^{0.42}$ K (illustrative).

    The Mode Counter counts the standing waves of a perfectly conducting cube exactly: a triple $(n_x, n_y, n_z)$ with all three nonzero has two polarizations, one with a single zero has one, and one with two zeros has none. The count approaches $(8π/3)Vν^3/c^3$ as ν grows (0.9 % fewer at 300 THz in a 10 µm cube): for light the walls’ terms cancel, leaving a term from the cube’s edges, about $3Lν/c$, and the lattice’s scatter, so at some frequencies the count is above the formula. A thermal sample gives each mode of one band a random number of quanta from Planck’s geometric distribution, seeded by the press.

    Stars are blackbodies at their effective temperatures, with approximate published luminosities (below); the radius follows from $L = 4πR^2σT^4$ with the IAU’s nominal Sun, $L_⊙ = 3.828 × 10^{26}$ W, $R_⊙ = 6.957 × 10^8$ m and $T_⊙$ = 5,772 K. B − V is the blackbody’s color through Gaussian stand-ins for the B (440 nm, 97 nm wide) and V (550 nm, 88 nm wide) bands, counting photons, with its zero point set so the Sun gives 0.65: approximate, and shown beside each star’s catalog value, which differs both ways: the zero point is tied to the Sun, whose own lines redden it, and real stars’ continua and lines are not a blackbody’s. The CMB is a 2.725 48 K blackbody (Fixsen 2009).

    What the model leaves out

    Anything between the body and the viewer: no atmosphere, no glass, no dust. Emissivity’s dependence on angle, surface finish and temperature (the selective curves are illustrative). Stars’ absorption lines, the Balmer jump, limb darkening and every departure from a blackbody, which is why the model’s B − V differs from a star’s catalog value. The eye’s adaptation beyond one tone-mapping, the CIE observer’s person-to-person variation, and displays that differ from sRGB. The thermal camera’s optics and calibration and the air’s own infrared. The spectrometer’s stray light, second-order light, wavelength errors and read noise. The cavity’s walls as anything but perfect conductors, and the count’s surface and edge corrections beyond the formula. Anything out of equilibrium: lasers, fluorescence, LEDs and the line emission of flames.

    Sources

    Samuel J. Ling, Jeff Sanny and William Moebs, University Physics Volume 3 (OpenStax), §6.1 Blackbody Radiation, which the Intro track follows; Andrew Fraknoi, David Morrison and Sidney C. Wolff, Astronomy 2e (OpenStax), §5.2 (Wien’s and Stefan’s laws for stars), §17.2 (color indices), §18.3 (stars’ radii) and §18.4 (the H–R diagram); University Physics Volume 2 (OpenStax), ch. 1, the mechanisms of heat transfer, for emissivity and net exchange; all CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. M. Planck, Annalen der Physik 4, 553 (1901). E. Tiesinga et al., CODATA recommended values (2018), for σ and b. CIE 015:2018 Colorimetry, 4th ed., for the color-matching functions and Illuminant A; B. Kim et al., J. Korean Phys. Soc. (2002), for the Planckian locus check. IEC 61966-2-1 for sRGB. D. J. Fixsen, ApJ 707, 916 (2009), for 2.725 48 K. IAU 2015 Resolution B3 for the Sun. The stars (effective temperature, luminosity in L⊙): Proxima Centauri 3,040 K, 0.0016; Betelgeuse 3,600 K, about 1.2 × 10⁵; Arcturus 4,290 K, 170; Vega 9,600 K, 40; Sirius A 9,940 K, 25.4; Rigel 12,100 K, 1.2 × 10⁵; Sirius B 25,000 K, 0.026; catalog B − V from SIMBAD. These are approximate values from the literature, to be checked before release.

    Clip Capture

    The Clip Capture group in the top bar, on the tabs that can record, makes video clips and pictures for your slides. Pick 720p or 1080p: the clip is that size whatever your window. ⏺ Rerun restarts the scene from the beginning and records it; ⏺ Record starts from where it is now. Keep using the controls while it records. It stops at Stop, after 60 seconds, or when you change tabs, then offers the clip to download; the ▶ button shows it again. The camera button saves a still picture (PNG).

    Clips are MP4 in Chrome, Edge and Safari and WebM in Firefox, and carry a small, faint glidepathscience.org tag in the corner. They are made on your computer and never uploaded.

    Sharing

    A single self-contained HTML file. Copy it anywhere: email, thumb drive, shared drive, LMS. It opens in any modern browser with no installer, no network and no telemetry.

    For graded work, end the link with ?predict=assessed: the Predict Lab then opens in Assessed mode (one try a round), and the session report adds the Assessed rounds alone, level by level. The link is read when the page opens; nothing is stored.
